# What to do

Every group has a **different** set of clauses. There is no one right answer
across the room — that is the point.

A clause is an OR of literals. All the clauses must hold at once.

**The loop.** Repeat until you cannot:

1. Find a clause with **exactly one literal**. That literal must be true.
   **Circle it** — call it a **unit**.
2. Look for that same literal in any other clause. That clause is already
   satisfied, so **circle the literal there too, and cross the whole clause
   out.** The circle records why it went.
3. In every clause containing the **negation** of your unit, strike out just
   that one literal. The rest of the clause stays.
4. If a clause loses its **last** literal, **circle what is left of it**. That is
   **⊥**, the empty clause — a clause with no way left to be true. Finding one is
   the best thing that can happen to you.

A circle always marks something you have **established**: a literal that must be
true, or — best of all — an empty clause. A crossed-out clause always has a
circle in it saying which literal did the work.

**Stop when** one of three things happens, and say which:

| | |
|---|---|
| You reach **⊥** | the clauses contradict each other |
| **No clauses are left** | everything is settled, and consistently |
| **No clause has a single literal**, but clauses remain | nothing further is forced |

All three are real answers. Finding out which one you have *is* the exercise.

## Set 1

| | Clause | Working |
|:-:|---|---|
| 1 | $\{\neg A\}$ | |
| 2 | $\{\neg B,\ \neg D,\ \neg G\}$ | |
| 3 | $\{\neg E\}$ | |
| 4 | $\{\neg C,\ E,\ F\}$ | |
| 5 | $\{A,\ \neg C,\ E,\ \neg F\}$ | |
| 6 | $\{C,\ E\}$ | |
